paper_title: DeLoop: Repeated Actions as Self-Supervision for Long-Horizon Agents

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Language-model agents that run long tasks often redo work they have already done: they re-issue a tool call they made earlier and get back exactly the same observation, a step that adds no new information. We identify this failure as a loop. Loops appear natively in Qwen, Llama, and Gemini agents and become far more common once the agent's history is compressed to fit its context window. To reduce these loops, we propose DeLoop, a self-supervised training method. DeLoop builds on a simple observation: the agent's own rollout can provide the supervision needed to learn from its loops. We use a looping action as a negative example and the first later non-looping action in the same rollout as a positive example. DeLoop learns from these pairs through direct preference optimization and does not require task rewards, gold answers, or LLM judges. On CodeGym under compression, DeLoop reduces the share of Qwen3-8B tasks containing loops from 57.3% to 6.1%. It also uses about one third as many steps per task, with similar task success. On Qwen3-32B, DeLoop reduces loops and steps while raising task success from 37.7% to 44.8%.

Keywords: LLM agents, long-horizon agents, agent memory, context compression, agent loops, repeated actions, preference optimization 1. Introduction Language-model agents increasingly solve tasks over long interaction horizons: they inspect repositories, execute commands, call tools, and act on environment feedback across many steps (Du et al., 2025; Jimenez et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024a; Yao et al., 2023). Yet they often redo work they have already done. The agent calls the same tool with the same arguments, receives the same observation, and then issues the same call again (Figure 1). Each repeated call is looping action: it gets back an observation the agent already has and adds no new information. We formulate this failure as loop. The failure is already present even when the full, uncompressed history is available, but compression makes it worse. On CodeGym (Du et al., 2025), the loop rate of Qwen3-8B (Yang et al., 2025), the share of tasks with at least one loop, rises from 29.0% with the full history (no summarization) to 57.3% under summarization, while looping actions per task increase more than 3.5! More importantly, in addition to wasted tool calls, we empirically observed that trajectories that enter loop fail in all six Qwen3 and Gemini models we evaluate: on average, 59.5% of looping runs fail, compared with 33.4% of loop-free runs (Figure 2). Thus, context compression makes looping more likely and increases the chances of task failure. Recent work manages growing interaction histories through external memory (Fox et al., 2026; Packer et al., 2023), hierarchical or summarized working context (Hu et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2025), compact learned state (Zhou et al., 2025), and learned context compression or management (Kang et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2026). These works study what history should an agent retain to continue acting well under bounded context window. In contrast, we study complementary question about how the agents policy uses its history after compression. That is, when the history records an action, does the agent use that record to avoid repeating it? We find that most agents do so only partly. Another way to reduce looping is to improve the agents policy. Some methods address agent failures at inference time through reflection (Shinn et al., 2023) or early stopping (Lu et al., 2025). Others train agents using demonstrations (Chen et al., 2023; Zeng et al., 2024), search-based training data (Yuan et al., 2025), or step-level supervision (Chen and Yuille, 2026; Tang, 2026; Xiong et al., 2024). We instead ask: can the failure itself provide useful signal to improve agents policy? Based on these observations, we propose DeLoop, self-supervised training method. Our key observation is that loops can provide their own training signal. We note that loop is simple trajectory-level event that can be identified directly from the action-observation trace, without requiring post-hoc failure attribution (Barke et al., 2026; 2026 Google. (Right) Qwen3-8B on CodeGym: DeLoop and the baseline summarize at 4,096 tokens; full history is the uncompressed reference. Hou et al., 2026). Within single rollout, we pair looping action with the first later non-looping action that differs from it. The looping action provides natural negative, while the later action provides positive signal. Figure 1 illustrates this. These pairs are mined directly from the interaction, without gold answers, LLM judges, external rewards, or task-success labels. We train the policy on these pairs through direct preference optimization (DPO Rafailov et al., 2023). On Qwen3-8B, DeLoop cuts the loop rate 9.4 while lowering interaction cost, with similar task success. On Qwen3-32B, the self-mined pairs alone reduce loop rate from 38.5% to 12.9% and raise task success from 37.7% to 44.8%, while also lowering interaction cost. Adding cross-domain pairs (DeLoop-Mix) raises Qwen3-8B task success from 25.1% to 30.3%. Our contributions are: 1. Identifying loops in long-horizon agents: we identify and characterize loops, simple failure in which an agent repeats an earlier action and receives the same observation. We show that loops occur even with the full history, grow sharply under compression, and are associated with task failure. 2. Mining loop actions as self-supervision: we introduce simple mining method that turns discovered loops into preference pairs from the agents own rollouts, with no external supervision. 3. Reducing loops in long-horizon agents: DeLoop reduces loops (57.3% to 6.1% on Qwen38B) while lowering interaction cost. The gains also extend to larger models, where there is pronounced improvement in task success (45.1% to 52.3% on Qwen3-14B and 37.7% to 44.8% on Qwen3-32B). 2. Related work Repeated actions in agents. Repetition is known failure of LLM agents. AgentBench found that agents mainly exceed their task limit because they repeat earlier content (Liu et al., 2024). MAST also lists step repetition as failure mode of multi-agent systems (Cemri et al., 2025), and RAGEN shows that multi-turn RL can trap agents in repetitive reasoning (Wang et al., 2025b). Closest to our setting, Min et al. (2026) find that repeated context compression increases repeated exploration and improve the compression prompt to reduce it; we keep the compressor fixed and change the policy. IAL-Scan finds code paths that can run without bound (Hou et al., 2026), and other work locates agent failures in execution traces (Barke et al., 2026; Deshpande et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026; Yeh et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2025). At inference time, agents can reflect, stop early, or escalate to stronger model (He et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2025; Shinn et al., 2023). OpenHands flags an agent as stuck when the same 2 DeLoop: Repeated Actions as Self-Supervision for Long-Horizon Agents action returns the same observation four times in row (Wang et al., 2025a). These methods do not change the agent policy. Even with blocker that refuses repeated calls and returns their earlier result, Qwen3-8B on CodeGym still proposes an already executed call in 71.3% of tasks, as often as without the blocker (69.8%); DeLoop lowers this to 13.6% (Appendix J.2). We define loop as repeated tool call that returns the same observation. Loops persist even with summaries designed to keep past actions (Section 3.3), so we train the agent policy itself to break the loop. Context management. Long-horizon agents need to fit their history into limited context. Common context management methods store the history in external memory or searchable logs (Fox et al., 2026; Packer et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2026b), summarize older interactions (Hu et al., 2025; Su et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2025), keep compact learned state (Zhou et al., 2025), learn what to keep (Kang et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2026), or validate their summaries (Chen et al., 2026). However, removing plans from the context sharply hurts performance (Mehta and Datta, 2026). These methods decide what history to keep. We instead ask whether the agent uses the kept history to avoid repeating actions. Learning from agent trajectories. Most methods that train agents on trajectories need an external signal to pick the better action. Agent tuning uses filtered or teacher-generated trajectories (Chen et al., 2023; Fu et al., 2025; Zeng et al., 2024), or successful attempts and outcome feedback (Guo et al., 2025; Jung et al., 2025; Le et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024b; Zelikman et al., 2022). ETO and Agentic-DPO take the better action from experts (Chen and Yuille, 2026; Song et al., 2024). Step-DPO, IPR, and ToolGraph use step-level labels or rewards (Lai et al., 2024; Tang, 2026; Xiong et al., 2024). Agent-R and Agent use tree search guided by rewards or critiques (Putta et al., 2024; Yuan et al., 2025), and SCoRe trains self-correction with online RL (Kumar et al., 2025). DeLoop instead takes the better action from the agents own later recovery in the same rollout and trains with DPO (Rafailov et al., 2023). Its only label is the exact-repeat rule of Section 3.1, so it needs no rewards, expert actions, or step labels. Like hindsight experience 3 replay (Andrychowicz et al., 2017), it also learns from failed rollouts. Penalizing repetition. Repetition can also be penalized directly. RLTR adds penalty on redundant tool calls to its reward (Li et al., 2025). In text generation, penalized sampling (Keskar et al., 2019), unlikelihood training (Welleck et al., 2020), and DITTO (Xu et al., 2022) reduce repeated tokens and sentences. These penalties mark what to avoid; DeLoop also supplies the agents own alternative action. Using our loop flag as per-step penalty in online RL (GRPO) lowers the Qwen38B loop rate on CodeGym from 57.3% to 15.0%, against 6.1% for DeLoop (Section 5.3). 3. Loops in Long-Horizon Agents 3.1. Defining Loop loop occurs when the agent repeats previous tool call with identical arguments and receives the same observation. Thus, that step adds no new information. For example, consider an agent counting clusters of online servers on grid. The agent has tools to find unvisited servers and mark them as visited. In one rollout, it issues the same search three times without marking the returned server. Because that server remains unmarked, each call returns the same coordinates. The latter two calls therefore add no new information. This rollout comes from Qwen3-8B agent on CodeGym (Du et al., 2025), where agents solve tasks through sequences of tool calls. We then label any run containing at least one looping action as looping run. We report the percentage of looping runs as the loop rate. 3.2. Loops Are Costly Each looping action consumes tokens and tool execution without yielding new observation. Under fixed interaction budget, these repeated calls leave fewer opportunities to take actions that could advance the task. We compare looping and loopfree Qwen3-8B runs on CodeGym under summarization at 4,096 tokens. Both groups include successful and failed runs. Looping runs contain 6.5 looping actions on average. They execute 10.5 more actions per task on average than loop-free runs. Their interaction transcripts also contain 11k more tokens. The same pattern holds for all six models in the cost comparison (Appendix Figure 7). Within each models compressed setting, looping runs are also more likely to fail than loop-free runs (Figure 2). The gap appears in all six Qwen3 and Gemini models: Qwen3-8B fails 85% of looping runs against 68% of loop-free runs. Gemini 3.1 Pro shows wider gap: 48% against 12%. loop thus marks run that is more likely to fail and has higher execution cost. 3.3. Compression Makes Loops More Common An agents interaction history records what it has already done. To keep long rollouts within context budget, the agent summarizes earlier interactions (Appendix D). We examine whether this compression makes the agent more likely to repeat completed actions. On CodeGym, Qwen3-8B loops in 29.0% of runs with the full history. Summarization at 4,096 tokens raises the loop rate to 57.3%. Lowering the threshold to 2,048 tokens raises it further to 64.7% (Figure 3a). The same pattern appears in all three Gemini models that we run with and without compression (Figure 3b). We compare CodeGym runs with the full history against the subset of summarization runs in which compression fires. Gemini 3.1 Pro loops least with the full history yet shows the largest increase, 2.9. To investigate this increase, we ask whether removing completed actions record makes the agent more likely to repeat it. We reconstruct 300 histories from 253 CodeGym tasks after compression. One version of each history keeps the most recent completed tool call and its observation. The other removes this record. We sample the next action eight times from each version. The agent repeats that call in 3.3% of samples with the record present and 48.8% with it removed (Appendix F). The record therefore helps the agent avoid an immediate repeat. This explains why compression causes more loops. However, over whole episode, keeping the record is not enough: Qwen3-8B still loops in 29.0% of runs with the full history. Under compression, quarter of runs (25.2%) repeat call that is still in the context word for word (Appendix J.1). Better context management does not close this gap. Summaries that keep an explicit record of past actions, such as trace of every executed call or ledger of tried actions, still loop in 52.0% to 62.7% of runs, close to standard summarization at 57.3% (Appendix Table 4). The compressors ACON (Kang et al., 2026) and LLMLingua-2 (Pan et al., 2024) lower the loop rate to 46.3% and 46.7%, still well above the 29.0% with the full history. The agent often fails to use record it has, so we train the policy itself (Section 4). Preference Training We train the policy πθ to prefer the chosen action over the looping action under the same context x. We use direct preference optimization (DPO; Rafailov et al., 2023), with the frozen base policy πref as the reference: (cid:16) = log σ πref (y+x) β log πθ(yx) β log πθ(y+x) πref (yx) (cid:17) . For Qwen3-8B, we train for one epoch with LoRA DPO (β = 0.05) on 8,000 self-mined CodeGym pairs. For Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B, we use the same mining rule and β, with pairs mined from each models own rollouts (Sections G.1 and G.17). At inference time, we use the trained policy throughout the rollout to generate each next action. In our standard setting, the harness triggers compression when the estimated history exceeds 4,096 tokens. The same trained model summarizes older interactions under separate prompt. It then continues acting from the updated context (Appendix D). DPO directly trains action preferences. Summary generation shares the updated weights but has no separate training objective. 5. Robustness and Generalization The CodeGym results show that self-mined pairs reduce loops and interaction cost. We now test whether these gains extend to other context settings, memory policies, and agent environments. 8 DeLoop: Repeated Actions as Self-Supervision for Long-Horizon Agents 6.3. The Repair Transfers to New Benchmarks Finally, we test DeLoop and DeLoop-Mix in native agent harnesses with different tools and interactions. Terminal-Bench tests terminal tasks, and BrowseComp-Plus tests web research. On Terminal-Bench, DeLoop cuts unproductive duplicate calls from 16.6 to 6.9 per task. On all 830 BrowseComp-Plus queries, DeLoop-Mix lowers the loop rate from 22.4% to 1.2% while matching the untrained models accuracy; DeLoop, trained on CodeGym pairs alone, already lowers it to 6.4%. We also test zero-shot transfer from CodeGym to ALFWorld. DeLoop on Qwen3-32B, trained only on CodeGym pairs, lowers the ALFWorld loop rate from 64.9% to 54.5% and raises task success from 33.6% to 42.5%. 7. Conclusion Long-horizon agents that compress their history fall into loops: they re-issue an action they already ran and receive the same result. On CodeGym, summarizing the history raises the loop rate of Qwen3-8B from 29.0% to 57.3%, and better context management alone does not remove it. Our key observation is that the loop labels itself: the looping action is the rejected action, and the agents later loop-breaking action is the chosen one. Trained on these self-mined pairs, DeLoop cuts the loop rate 9.4, from 57.3% to 6.1%, at about one third of the steps per task while maintaining task success, and raises task success by 7.2 points at 14B and 7.1 points at 32B. An agents own loops become its supervision: break the loop, keep the progress. We believe our work could help the community better understand and reduce loops in long-horizon agents.

Extension Studies We report four further studies on Qwen3-8B in CodeGym: what the policy conditions on (Section I.1), why the detector uses exact repetition (Section I.2), random-pair control (Section I.3), and what the chosen action adds (Section I.4). 26 I.1. The Policy Reacts to the Record of Its Own Executed Action We probe the moments at which the agent loops. Unlike the training-side points of Section F, these come from the compressed baselines runs on the 300 evaluation tasks: 150 looping points, one per task at its first loop. We add 80 retry points, at which an earlier call to the same action returned different observation, so calling it again is reasonable. At each point we rebuild the context from the raw history in six conditions: not yet executed (the history before the action was first run); proposed only (the same history plus note that the action was proposed but not run, padded to the same length); proposed + observation (the note also states what the action would return); just executed (the history ending right after the actions first run); record present (the full history up to the decision point); and record deleted (the same history with the record of the earlier run removed). We sample eight completions per condition at temperature 0.7 and report the re-issue rate, the share of completions whose next action is the probed action  (Table 25)  . Untrained policy. Planning an action does not stop the agent from issuing it: with the action only proposed, the untrained Qwen3-8B re-issues it in 73.9% of completions, the same as before the action was ever run (73.7%). Stating the observation lowers re-issue to 29.0%, and the record of the agents own execution lowers it further, to 16.5%. Deleting that record brings re-issue back to 53.3%. The effect is strongest right after the run (4.9%) and fades as history accumulates. The record also separates loops from reasonable retries. At retry points it lowers re-issue only from 68.4% to 51.7%, while stated observation alone lowers it to 20.6% and blocks retries that are worth making. The executed record, together with what it returned, is what tells the policy whether an action is finished or worth checking again. Trained policies. Both trained policies still tell loops from retries. With the record present, DeLoop re-issues looping action in 8.3% of completions and DeLoop-Mix in 6.8%, against 36.1% and 38.0% at retry points. Compression Amplifies Exact Repetition Most Our detector flags only exact repeats with an identical observation. We measure four broader signatures on the same CodeGym runs: near-duplicate calls (same tool, different arguments, with an identical observation or small argument edit), argument thrash (ABA argument alternation within three calls), redundant observe (an action whose observation is already in context, word for word, from different action), and productive repeats (the same action with different observation). Table 26 gives the results. Exact loops are the signature that compression amplifies most. Under summarization, their share of actions rises 3.77, from 6.6% to 24.8%, while every broader signature changes by 0.73 to 1.21. Near-duplicate and redundant-observe calls are common, in 77.9% and 56.3% of compressed tasks, but they behave like ordinary reprobing: with the full history they are more frequent in solved tasks (failure odds ratios 0.68 and 0.69). We therefore define the loop as exact repetition. Training lowers every signature per action, so the trained policies do not trade exact loops for near-duplicates: near-duplicate calls fall from 34.3% of actions to 19.0% under DeLoop and 23.7% under DeLoop-Mix. I.3. Random Pairs Do Not Break the Loop Does the loop label matter, or would any preference pair from the agents own rollouts do? We build random-pair corpus from the compressed baselines CodeGym rollouts: each pair keeps prompt and takes as its chosen and rejected actions two random later actions from the same rollout. We train on 877 random pairs and on random subsets of our 8,000 self-mined pairs with the same DPO recipe, match the number of optimizer updates to our main recipe (about 500), and evaluate on separate 128-task held-out CodeGym set  (Table 27)  .
